85310.e: Cardboard is collected like paper and made into new cardboard. Yoghurt pots are made of plastic and do not belong there.
85310.m: Cardboard boxes go to the cardboard collection.

85311.q: What is a Brockenhaus in Switzerland?
85311.e: At a Brockenhaus, also called a Brocki, you can drop off and buy used furniture, clothes and crockery. That way things are used again instead of thrown away.
85311.m: At the Brocki, old things get a second life.

85312.q: Which colour should you put a blue glass bottle with?
85312.e: There is no separate container for blue or red glass. Other colours go with green glass, because green glass copes best with other colours.
85312.m: Coloured glass goes with green glass.

85313.q: What does NOT belong in the bottle bank?
85313.e: Only bottles and jars for food belong in the bottle bank. Mirrors, window glass or drinking glasses melt differently and spoil the recycling.
85313.m: Only bottles and food jars belong in the bottle bank.

85314.q: What do you do with the lid before putting a jar in the bottle bank?
85314.e: Lids are usually made of metal and do not belong with the glass. You take them off and put them in the metal collection.
85314.m: Take the lid off before recycling a jar.

85315.q: On which day are you usually not allowed to use bottle banks in Switzerland?
85315.e: Throwing glass in is noisy. That is why it is forbidden on Sundays and at night in most municipalities.
85315.m: On Sunday the bottle bank stays quiet.

85316.q: What is made from melted waste glass?
85316.e: Waste glass is crushed, melted and shaped into bottles and jars again. That uses less energy than making brand new glass.
85316.m: Old glass is made into new bottles.

85317.q: How often can glass be recycled?
85317.e: Glass does not lose its quality when it is melted down. That is why it can be made into new glass again and again.
85317.m: Glass can be recycled again and again.

85318.q: What is the most important raw material for glass?
85318.e: Glass is mainly made from quartz sand, which is melted at very high temperatures. Collecting waste glass saves sand and energy.
85318.m: Glass is mainly made from sand.

85319.q: What is a PET bottle made of?
85319.e: PET is a type of plastic. It is light and does not break easily.
85319.m: PET bottles are made of plastic.

85320.q: Where can you return empty PET drinks bottles in Switzerland?
a: In the PET collection box in shops
85320.e: Almost everywhere that sells drinks in PET bottles has a collection box. You can return the empty bottles there for free.
85320.m: You take empty PET bottles back to the shop.

85321.q: What goes in the PET collection?
85321.e: Only drinks bottles go in the PET collection. Other plastic packaging spoils the recycling.
85321.m: Only drinks bottles go in the PET collection.

85322.q: What do you do with an empty PET bottle before putting it in?
85322.e: Squashed bottles take up less space. More bottles fit in a collection bag and fewer journeys are needed.

85323.q: What are collected PET bottles often made into?
85323.e: The collected PET is cleaned, shredded and melted. New drinks bottles are made from it.
85323.m: Old PET bottles become new PET bottles.

85324.q: Apart from bottles, what can be made from recycled PET?
85324.e: PET can be spun into fine threads. These are used, for example, to make fleece fabric for jumpers and jackets.
85324.m: PET can also be made into fabric for clothes.

85325.q: Why is PET recycling good for the environment?
85325.e: New PET is made from crude oil. Recycling PET means less oil and less energy are needed.

85326.q: Why should a PET bottle never be left lying in nature?
85326.e: Plastic hardly breaks down in nature. A bottle thrown away stays there for a very long time and harms animals.
85326.m: Plastic in nature stays for a very long time.

85327.e: Plant waste such as fruit, vegetables and leaves goes on the compost. Over time it turns into new soil.
85327.m: Fruit and vegetable scraps go on the compost.

85328.e: Earthworms eat the plant waste and loosen everything up. Their droppings are a very good fertiliser.
85328.m: Earthworms are busy helpers in the compost.

85329.q: What does a compost heap turn into?
85329.e: In the compost, plant waste turns into dark, rich soil. You can use it to feed plants in the garden.

85330.q: What does NOT belong on the garden compost?
85330.e: Cooked food and meat attract rats and other animals. That is why they do not belong on the garden compost.
85330.m: Meat scraps do not belong on the compost.

85331.q: What is the collection of garden and kitchen waste called in Switzerland?
85331.e: Many municipalities collect green waste such as grass cuttings, branches and vegetable peelings. It is made into compost or biogas.
85331.m: Green waste is waste from the garden and kitchen.

85332.q: What do tiny fungi and bacteria do in the compost?
85332.e: Fungi and bacteria are so small you can hardly see them. They break the plant waste down into tiny pieces.
85332.m: Tiny living things break down the compost.

85333.q: What can be produced from green waste in a biogas plant?
85333.e: In a biogas plant, bacteria break down the green waste without air. This produces gas that can be used to make electricity and heat.
85333.m: Green waste can be made into biogas.

85334.q: How long does it take for garden waste to turn into compost?
85334.e: The living things in the compost work slowly. It usually takes several months to about a year until the compost is ready.
85334.m: Good compost needs a few months.

85335.q: What is the bag for normal household waste called in Switzerland?
85335.e: Waste that cannot be recycled goes in the rubbish bag. It is picked up by the rubbish collection.
85335.m: Household waste goes in the rubbish bag.

85336.q: Why do rubbish bags cost extra in many Swiss municipalities?
85336.e: If you make a lot of rubbish, you need more bags and pay more. This is meant to encourage people to avoid waste and separate recyclables.

85337.q: Where do the contents of the rubbish bag go in Switzerland?
85337.e: In Switzerland, the waste from rubbish bags is burnt in a waste incineration plant. It is called a KVA for short.

85338.q: What is produced when waste is burnt in an incineration plant?
85338.e: The heat from burning is put to use. It makes electricity and heats homes through pipes.
85338.m: Burning waste produces heat and electricity.

85339.q: Where does an empty metal tin go?
85339.e: Tins are made of sheet metal. Scrap metal can be melted down and used again.
85339.m: Metal tins go to the metal collection.

85340.q: Where should a pair of trousers in good condition that has become too small go?
85340.e: Good clothes can be put in collection bins or passed on. That way other people can still wear them.
85340.m: Good clothes go to the clothes collection.

85341.q: What helps most to avoid waste?
85341.e: A water bottle can be refilled many times. That means fewer disposable bottles and cups are needed.
85341.m: Reusing is better than throwing away.

85342.q: What is it called when you simply drop rubbish on the ground?
85342.e: Littering means carelessly leaving or throwing away rubbish. In many Swiss towns you can be fined for it.
85342.m: Rubbish belongs in the bin, not on the ground.

85343.q: Where do empty aluminium coffee capsules go?
a: To the aluminium or capsule collection
85343.e: Aluminium coffee capsules can be returned at collection points or in shops. The aluminium is recycled.

85344.q: Where do you take used batteries in Switzerland?
85344.e: In Switzerland, shops that sell batteries must take old batteries back. They have collection boxes.
85344.m: You take used batteries back to the shop.

85345.q: Why do batteries not belong in the rubbish bag?
85345.e: Batteries contain substances that can harm the environment. When recycled, they are handled safely.
85345.m: Batteries contain substances that must not get into the environment.

85346.q: How much does it cost to return old batteries to a shop?
85346.e: When you buy a battery, you already pay a small fee for recycling. That is why returning it is free.

a: A battery you can charge again
85347.e: A rechargeable battery can be charged again and again. When it no longer holds its charge, it goes to the collection point like a normal battery.
85347.m: A rechargeable battery is a battery you can recharge.

85348.q: Why are old lithium batteries dangerous in household rubbish?
85348.e: Damaged lithium batteries can get very hot and catch fire. That is why they belong in the battery collection.
85348.m: Lithium batteries can burn and belong at the collection point.

85349.q: What can be recovered from old batteries?
a: Metals such as zinc and iron
85349.e: In battery recycling the metals are separated. Zinc, iron and other metals can be used again.
85349.m: Metals are recovered from old batteries.

85350.q: Which symbol on batteries shows that they do not belong in the rubbish?
85350.e: The crossed-out wheelie bin means the item does not belong in normal rubbish. You find it on batteries and electrical devices.
85350.m: A crossed-out wheelie bin means it does not go in the rubbish.

85351.q: Why must button batteries be kept away from small children?
85351.e: Small children could swallow a button battery. That can cause serious injuries inside the body.
85351.m: Keep button batteries out of reach of small children.

85352.q: Which animals often mistake plastic bags in the sea for jellyfish?
85352.e: Sea turtles like to eat jellyfish. A plastic bag in the water looks similar and can make them ill.
85352.m: Plastic bags in the sea are dangerous for turtles.

85353.q: How does a lot of plastic waste get into the sea?
85353.e: Rubbish dropped on land often ends up in streams and rivers. They carry it all the way to the sea.
85353.m: Rivers carry rubbish all the way to the sea.

85354.q: What is a huge collection of plastic waste in the ocean called?
85354.e: Ocean currents turn in circles and collect rubbish there. This creates large garbage patches.
85354.m: Ocean currents gather plastic into garbage patches.

85355.q: In which ocean is the largest known garbage patch?
85355.e: The largest known garbage patch lies in the North Pacific between Hawaii and California. It is called the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.
85355.m: The largest garbage patch is in the Pacific.

85356.q: How long does a plastic bottle take to break down in the sea?
85356.e: In the sea, plastic breaks down only very slowly into smaller and smaller pieces. Experts estimate this can take hundreds of years.
85356.m: Plastic stays in the sea for hundreds of years.

85357.q: Why is plastic dangerous for seabirds?
85357.e: Seabirds think pieces of plastic are food and eat them. Their stomach is then full, but the bird gets no nourishment.
85357.m: Seabirds can die from swallowed plastic.

85358.q: What is a lost fishing net drifting in the sea called?
85358.e: Ghost nets drift ownerless in the sea. Fish, dolphins and turtles can get caught in them.
85358.m: Lost fishing nets are called ghost nets.

85359.q: Via which river can rubbish from Switzerland reach the North Sea?
85359.e: The Rhine flows from Switzerland through Germany and the Netherlands into the North Sea. Rubbish in the Rhine can reach the sea this way.
85359.m: The Rhine flows into the North Sea.

85360.e: Microplastics are very small pieces of plastic. They are found in water, in soil and in the air.
85360.m: Microplastics are tiny bits of plastic.

85361.q: Up to what size are bits of plastic called microplastic?
85361.e: Plastic pieces smaller than 5 millimetres are called microplastic. Many are so small you cannot see them.

85362.q: Where does a lot of microplastic in Switzerland come from?
85362.e: When driving, car tyres wear down on the road. The fine particles end up in soil and water.
85362.m: Car tyres lose tiny particles when driving.

85363.q: Which clothes lose a lot of microplastic when washed?
85363.e: Fleece is made of plastic fibres. When washed, tiny fibres come loose and end up in the waste water.
85363.m: Clothes made of synthetic fibres lose microplastic when washed.

85364.q: Where has microplastic already been found?
a: In the sea, in lakes and in soil
85364.e: Microplastic has spread almost everywhere. Researchers have found it in the sea, in Swiss lakes and even in snow.
85364.m: Microplastic is almost everywhere on Earth.

85365.q: What can you use to see very small microplastic?
85365.e: Many particles are smaller than a grain of sand. With a microscope you can see them magnified.
85365.m: Under a microscope you can see tiny bits of plastic.

85366.q: What happens to a plastic bag that lies in the sun and water for a long time?
85366.e: Sunlight and waves make plastic brittle. It breaks into smaller and smaller pieces but does not disappear.
85366.m: Big pieces of plastic break down into microplastic.

85367.q: What helps to make less microplastic in the washing machine?
a: Wearing clothes made of natural fibres
85367.e: Clothes made of cotton or wool are not made of plastic. They do not release microplastic when washed.
85367.m: Natural fibres do not release microplastic.

85368.q: What does a sewage treatment plant do?
85368.e: In the sewage treatment plant, dirty water from homes is cleaned. Afterwards it can flow back into nature.
85368.m: The sewage treatment plant makes dirty water clean.

85369.q: What is a sewage treatment plant often called for short in Switzerland?
85369.e: ARA stands for Abwasserreinigungsanlage, a waste water treatment plant. Almost every municipality in Switzerland is connected to an ARA.
85369.m: In Switzerland, the sewage treatment plant is called ARA.

85370.q: Where does the water from the toilet go?
85370.e: Waste water flows through pipes in the sewers to the sewage treatment plant. There it is cleaned.
85370.m: Waste water flows through the sewers to the treatment plant.

85371.q: Who helps to clean the water in a sewage treatment plant?
85371.e: In the aeration tank, bacteria eat the dirt in the water. This makes the water cleaner.
85371.m: Bacteria eat the dirt in waste water.

85372.q: What should you never throw down the toilet?
85372.e: Cotton buds, wet wipes and other rubbish block pipes and cause problems at the treatment plant. They belong in the rubbish bag.
85372.m: Only toilet paper goes down the toilet.

85373.q: Where does the cleaned water from the treatment plant go?
a: Straight into the drinking water pipes
85373.e: The cleaned water is let into a stream, river or lake. It is clean enough for nature, but it is not drinking water.
85373.m: Cleaned waste water flows back into nature.

85374.q: What happens to sewage sludge in Switzerland?
a: It is dumped in the sea
85374.e: Sewage sludge can contain harmful substances. That is why in Switzerland it may no longer be spread on fields and is burnt instead.
85374.m: Sewage sludge is burnt in Switzerland.

85375.q: What is the large tank in a treatment plant called where gas is made from sludge?
85375.e: In the digester tower, bacteria break down the sludge without air. The gas that forms is used for electricity and heat.
85375.m: In the digester tower, gas is made from sewage sludge.

85376.e: Hazardous waste contains poisonous or dangerous substances. It must be collected separately and treated specially.
85376.m: Dangerous waste is called hazardous waste.

85377.e: Paints and varnishes contain substances that pollute water and soil. That is why you take them to the hazardous waste collection.

85379.q: How can you recognise dangerous substances on packaging?
a: By a diamond with a red border
85379.e: Hazard symbols are black pictures in a diamond with a red border. They warn, for example, of fire or poison.
85379.m: A red diamond warns of danger.

85380.q: Where do spray cans that still have paint in them go?
85380.e: Spray cans with leftovers are under pressure and contain chemicals. That is why they count as hazardous waste.
85380.m: Spray cans that are not empty are hazardous waste.

85381.q: Where do you take a broken mobile phone?
85381.e: Shops that sell electrical devices take old devices back for free. The valuable metals are recycled.
85381.m: You return old electrical devices to the shop.

85382.q: Why do energy-saving light bulbs not belong in the rubbish?
a: They keep glowing in the bag
85382.e: Energy-saving bulbs contain a small amount of poisonous mercury. That is why you return them to a shop or collection point.
85382.m: Energy-saving bulbs go to the collection point.

a: Making something new out of something old
Throwing new things away at once
85383.e: With upcycling, an old object becomes something new and useful. That way it does not become rubbish.
85383.m: With upcycling, old things get a new purpose.

85384.q: What is an example of upcycling?
a: Using a jam jar as a vase
Putting a jar in the bottle bank
85384.e: An empty jam jar can be used as a flower vase. The jar keeps being used.
85384.m: An old jar can get a new job.

85385.q: What can you sew from an old pair of jeans?
85385.e: Denim is very strong. You can sew a bag or a pencil case from old jeans.
85385.m: You can sew bags from old clothes.

85386.q: What can you make from an empty tin?
85386.e: A clean tin without sharp edges can be painted. Then it becomes a holder for colouring pencils.
85386.m: An old tin can become a pencil holder.

85387.q: What can you build from old wooden pallets?
85387.e: Wooden pallets are used for transporting goods. You can build shelves, tables or sofas from old pallets.
85387.m: Furniture can be built from wooden pallets.

85388.q: What is it called when recycling turns a material into something less valuable?
85388.e: With downcycling a material loses value, for example when good paper can only be made into cardboard. Upcycling is the opposite.
85388.m: Downcycling is the opposite of upcycling.

85389.q: What can you make from an old T-shirt?
85389.e: An old T-shirt made of soft fabric is good for cleaning. That way you do not need to buy new cloths.
85389.m: Old T-shirts make good cleaning cloths.

a: It breaks down into soil in nature
85390.e: Biodegradable things are eaten by tiny living things such as fungi and bacteria. In the end they turn back into soil.
85390.m: Biodegradable means it turns into soil in nature.

85391.e: A banana skin is part of a plant. It breaks down in nature, but glass, metal and plastic do not.

85392.q: Which of these breaks down fastest in nature?
85392.e: Paper is made from wood, so it can break down. Glass, plastic and aluminium stay much longer.
85392.m: Paper breaks down faster than plastic.

85393.q: What can biodegradable plastic be made from?
85393.e: Some plastics are made from plants such as maize. They are called bioplastics.
85393.m: Some plastics are made from plants.

85394.q: Which of these takes longest to disappear in nature?
85394.e: Glass is not broken down by living things. A glass bottle can lie in nature for many thousands of years.
85394.m: Glass stays in nature for an extremely long time.

85395.q: Why is chewing gum that has been thrown away a problem?
85395.e: Chewing gum today is mostly made of plastic. It sticks to streets and squares for years.
85395.m: Chewing gum belongs in the bin.

85396.e: Wood comes from trees and is broken down by fungi and bacteria. Plastic, steel and china are not.

85397.q: Which living things are especially good at breaking down dead wood in the forest?
85397.e: Fungi grow into dead wood and slowly make it soft and rotten. Over time it becomes new forest soil.

85398.q: What does the screen at the entrance to the treatment plant hold back?
85398.e: The screen is a grid with narrow bars. It catches large things such as rags, sticks and branches.
85398.m: The screen fishes large things out of the waste water.

85399.q: Why should a compost heap not dry out completely?
85399.e: Worms, fungi and bacteria can only work if it is damp enough. Good compost is as damp as a squeezed-out sponge.

85400.q: What can you make from an old bike inner tube?
85400.e: A bike inner tube is made of rubber and is very tough. You can make belts, purses or bags from it.
85400.m: You can make belts from bike inner tubes.

86273.q: Which gas makes party balloons float upwards?
86273.e: Helium is much lighter than air. That is why a balloon filled with helium floats upwards.
86273.m: A helium balloon rises because helium is lighter than air.

86274.q: What happens to a helium balloon after a few days?
86274.e: The helium slowly escapes through the skin of the balloon. That is why the balloon gets smaller and sinks to the ground.
86274.m: A helium balloon loses its gas over time.

86275.e: Helium is a noble gas and does not burn. That is why it is safe for balloons.
86275.m: Helium does not burn, so it is safe.

86276.q: Which object in the sky is helium named after?
86276.e: Helium was first discovered in the light of the Sun. ‘Helios’ is the Greek word for sun.
86276.m: Helium gets its name from the Sun.

86277.e: Helium is an invisible gas. You cannot see it.

86278.q: Why should you not breathe in helium from balloons?
a: You do not get enough oxygen
Your voice stays high for ever
86278.e: If you breathe in helium, not enough oxygen gets into your lungs. You can faint, and that is dangerous.
86278.m: Do not breathe in helium from balloons.

86279.q: What are modern airships filled with?
86279.e: Modern airships are filled with helium. It is light and does not burn.

86280.q: Which gas is the second lightest after hydrogen?
86280.e: Hydrogen is the lightest element. Helium comes straight after it.
86280.m: Helium is the second lightest element.

86281.e: Helium has no smell and no taste.

86282.q: What colour does neon glow in a tube light?
86282.e: When electricity flows through neon, it glows reddish orange. Other colours come from other gases or coloured tubes.

86283.q: What is neon at room temperature?
86283.e: Neon is a gas. You cannot see it at room temperature.

86284.q: Where is neon gas obtained from?
86284.e: There is a tiny amount of neon in the air. It is obtained by cooling air down a lot and separating it.
86284.m: Neon is obtained from the air.

86285.q: What does the name neon mean?
86285.e: ‘Neos’ means ‘new’ in Greek. Neon was newly discovered in 1898.
86285.m: The name neon means ‘the new one’.

86286.q: Which group of substances does neon belong to?
86286.e: Neon is a noble gas, like helium and argon. Noble gases hardly combine with other substances.
86286.m: Neon is one of the noble gases.

86287.e: Neon colours are loud and glowing, for example neon yellow. They are called that because they remind people of glowing neon tubes.
86287.m: Neon colours are bright and glowing.

86288.q: What are glowing advertising signs made of gas tubes called?
86288.e: Glowing writing made of bent glass tubes is called a neon sign. You see them on shops and cinemas.
86288.m: Neon signs glow in glass tubes.

a: Yes, even just looking at it
86289.e: Neon is not poisonous. It hardly reacts with other substances.

86290.q: What does a B on a pencil mean?
86290.e: B stands for ‘black’. A B pencil contains a lot of graphite and writes soft and dark.
86290.m: A B pencil writes soft and dark.

86291.q: What can you use to lubricate a sticking door lock?
86291.e: Graphite is smooth and lubricates without being sticky. That is why fine graphite powder helps with sticking locks.
86291.m: Graphite powder makes locks turn more easily.

86292.q: Why can you rub out pencil lines?
a: The graphite only lies on top of the paper
The line is made of water
86292.e: When you write, tiny bits of graphite stay on the paper. The rubber picks them up again.
86292.m: You can rub out pencil because the graphite only sits on top.

86293.e: Graphite is greyish black and a little shiny. That is why a pencil writes grey.

86294.e: The layers in graphite slide easily over each other. That is why it feels smooth and greasy.

86295.e: Graphite conducts electricity even though it is not a metal. That is why it is used in batteries, for example.

86296.q: Why is the core of a pencil called ‘lead’?
a: People used to think graphite was lead
It is as heavy as lead
Its casing used to be made of lead
86296.e: In the past, people thought graphite was a kind of lead. The name stuck, even though there is no lead in it.
86296.m: There is no lead in a pencil.

86297.q: What does the Greek word that ‘graphite’ comes from mean?
86297.e: ‘Graphein’ means ‘to write’ in Greek. You can write with graphite.
86297.m: Graphite comes from the Greek word for ‘to write’.

86298.q: Why is chlorine added to swimming pool water?
86298.e: Chlorine kills bacteria and other germs. That keeps the pool water clean.

86299.q: When does an indoor pool smell especially strongly of ‘chlorine’?
a: When there is a lot of sweat in the water
When the water is completely clean
When the sun is shining outside
When only a few people are swimming
86299.e: The typical pool smell forms when chlorine reacts with sweat, wee and dirt. That is why you shower before swimming.
86299.m: Showering before swimming helps against the chlorine smell.

86300.e: Pure chlorine is yellowish green. Its name comes from the Greek word for ‘yellowish green’.

86301.q: Which element is found together with sodium in table salt?
86301.e: The chemical name for table salt is sodium chloride. It is made of sodium and chlorine.
86301.m: Table salt is made of sodium and chlorine.

86302.q: What protects your eyes from chlorinated water when swimming?
86302.e: Chlorinated water can irritate the eyes. Swimming goggles keep the water away from your eyes.
86302.m: Swimming goggles protect your eyes in the pool.

86303.e: Pure chlorine is very poisonous. But in a swimming pool there is only a tiny amount of chlorine in the water.

86304.q: What can chlorinated water do to colourful swimwear?
86304.e: Chlorine bleaches colours. That is why swimwear gets paler over time.

86305.q: What is chlorine at room temperature?
86305.e: Pure chlorine is a gas at room temperature. It is heavier than air.

86306.q: What is fluoride in toothpaste good for?
86306.e: Fluoride makes tooth enamel harder. That way teeth do not get holes so quickly.

86307.q: About how much toothpaste do small children need?
86307.e: For small children, an amount the size of a pea is enough. That is enough to protect the teeth.
86307.m: Small children only need a pea-sized amount of toothpaste.

86308.q: What do you do with the toothpaste foam after brushing your teeth?
86308.e: You do not swallow toothpaste. You spit out the foam.

86309.q: Which food can you also buy with fluoride in Switzerland?
86309.e: In Switzerland there is table salt with iodine and fluoride. It helps to protect teeth.
86309.m: In Switzerland there is salt with fluoride.

86310.q: Which thing that you use every day contains fluoride?
86310.e: Fluoride in toothpaste makes teeth stronger. That is why you brush them with toothpaste.

86311.q: Which drink naturally contains quite a lot of fluoride?
86311.e: Tea plants take up fluoride from the soil. That is why black tea contains quite a lot of it.

86312.q: What is pure fluorine at room temperature?
86312.e: Pure fluorine is a pale yellow gas. It is very poisonous and reacts violently.
86312.m: Pure fluorine is a poisonous gas.

86313.q: What forms as a white layer in the kettle?
86313.e: Tap water contains dissolved lime. When it boils, the lime is left behind as a white layer.
86313.m: Limescale forms white crusts in the kettle.

86314.q: Which animals build huge reefs of lime in the sea?
86314.e: Corals are tiny animals. They build skeletons of lime, and these grow into large reefs.
86314.m: Coral reefs are made of lime.

86315.q: Which rock are the Jura mountains mostly made of?
86315.e: The Jura is mostly made of limestone. It formed long ago at the bottom of a sea.
86315.m: The Jura is made of limestone.

86316.q: What are seashells and snail shells made of?
86316.e: Mussels and snails build their shells from lime. They take the lime from the water or from their food.
86316.m: Mussels build their shells from lime.

86317.q: What is the shell of a hen's egg mainly made of?
86317.e: Eggshells are almost entirely made of lime. The hen needs a lot of lime from its food for this.

86318.q: What are stalactites and stalagmites in caves made of?
86318.e: Water with dissolved lime drips from the cave ceiling. The lime is left behind and grows very slowly into stalactites and stalagmites.
86318.m: Stalactites and stalagmites grow from lime.

86319.q: What is tap water with a lot of lime in it called?
86319.e: Water with a lot of lime is called hard water. Water with little lime is called soft water.
86319.m: Water with a lot of lime is called hard.

86320.q: What happens when you drip vinegar onto a piece of limestone?
86320.e: Vinegar is an acid and reacts with lime. A gas forms, and it fizzes.
86320.m: Limestone fizzes when vinegar touches it.

86321.q: Which gas forms when lime reacts with acid?
86321.e: Lime contains carbon and oxygen. With acid, it produces the gas carbon dioxide.
86321.m: Lime and acid give carbon dioxide.

86322.e: Pure sulphur is light yellow. It is found as yellow crystals.

86323.q: What do many substances containing sulphur smell of?
86323.e: Hydrogen sulphide smells of rotten eggs. Pure sulphur itself hardly smells.
86323.m: Some sulphur substances stink of rotten eggs.

86324.q: Where is sulphur often found in nature?
86324.e: Gases containing sulphur come out of volcanoes. Yellow sulphur settles there.
86324.m: Yellow sulphur is found at volcanoes.

86325.q: What is in the head of many matches?
86325.e: The head of many matches contains sulphur. It helps the wood catch fire.

86326.q: Is pure sulphur solid, liquid or a gas at room temperature?
86326.e: Pure sulphur is a solid. It only melts at about 115 degrees.

86327.q: In which town in the canton of Aargau does warm thermal water containing sulphur bubble up?
86327.e: In Baden, warm water comes out of the ground. It contains sulphur and many other minerals.
86327.m: Baden has thermal water containing sulphur.

86328.q: What colour flame does sulphur burn with?
86328.e: Sulphur burns with a blue flame. A gas with a sharp smell forms.

86329.q: Which letter is the symbol for sulphur?
86329.e: Sulphur is called ‘sulfur’ in Latin. That is why its symbol is S.
86329.m: The symbol for sulphur is S.

86330.e: Liquid nitrogen looks like water. But it is extremely cold and evaporates at once.

86331.q: Roughly how much of the air is nitrogen?
86331.e: Around 78 out of 100 parts of the air are nitrogen. That is about three quarters.
86331.m: About three quarters of the air is nitrogen.

86332.q: About how cold is liquid nitrogen?
86332.e: Nitrogen only becomes liquid at about minus 196 degrees. So it is extremely cold.

86333.q: Why does garden fertiliser often contain nitrogen?
a: So that the soil stays dry
86333.e: Plants need nitrogen to build leaves and stems. That is why fertiliser often contains nitrogen.

86334.q: What does our body do with the nitrogen from the air when we breathe?
86334.e: Our body does not need the nitrogen from the air. We simply breathe it out again.
86334.m: We breathe the nitrogen from the air out again.

86336.q: Which gas is often put in crisp packets to keep the crisps fresh?
86336.e: Nitrogen pushes the oxygen out of the packet. That way the crisps do not go stale so quickly.

86337.q: Which letter is the symbol for nitrogen?
86337.e: Nitrogen is called ‘nitrogenium’ in Latin. That is why its symbol is N.
86337.m: The symbol for nitrogen is N.

86338.q: What happens to a flower dipped in liquid nitrogen?
a: It bursts into bloom at once
86338.e: Liquid nitrogen is so cold that the flower freezes instantly. After that it shatters like glass.
86338.m: Liquid nitrogen makes flowers rock hard.

86339.q: What happens to an iron screw placed on mercury?
86339.e: Mercury is almost twice as heavy as iron. That is why iron floats on mercury like wood on water.

86340.e: Mercury shines silver like a mirror. That is why its old name is quicksilver.

86341.q: Which measuring device often used to contain mercury?
86341.e: In the past, mercury in a clinical thermometer showed your temperature. Today other thermometers are used.
86341.m: Clinical thermometers used to contain mercury.

86342.e: Mercury and its vapour are poisonous. That is why it is replaced wherever possible today.

86343.q: What do you do if an old mercury thermometer breaks?
a: Touch nothing and fetch an adult
Pick it up with your fingers
86343.e: Mercury is poisonous, so you do not touch it. Adults must get rid of it carefully.
86343.m: Do not touch mercury from a broken thermometer.

86344.q: Which planet has the same name as the metal mercury?
86344.e: In English the metal and the planet are both called mercury. In German, however, the metal is called Quecksilber.
86344.m: The metal mercury shares its name with the planet.

86346.q: What does mercury form when you pour it onto a table?
86346.e: Mercury pulls itself together into round beads. These roll around easily.

86347.q: What does our body need calcium for?
86347.e: Calcium makes bones and teeth hard and strong. Almost all the calcium in the body is in the bones.
86347.m: Calcium makes bones and teeth strong.

86348.q: Which drink provides a lot of calcium?
86348.e: Milk contains a lot of calcium. One glass of milk already covers a good part of what you need in a day.
86348.m: Milk provides a lot of calcium.

86349.q: Which food contains a lot of calcium?
86349.e: Cheese contains a lot of calcium. Hard cheese such as Sbrinz has especially lots.
86349.m: Cheese contains a lot of calcium.

86350.e: Pure calcium is a soft, silvery metal. In nature, however, it is only found in compounds.

86351.q: Which green vegetable contains a lot of calcium?
86351.e: Broccoli and other green cabbage vegetables contain a lot of calcium. Cucumbers have only a little.

86352.q: What is the symbol for calcium?
86352.e: The symbol for calcium is Ca. C stands for carbon and Cl for chlorine.
86352.m: The symbol for calcium is Ca.

86353.q: Which vitamin helps the body take in calcium?
86353.e: Vitamin D helps calcium from food get into the bones. Our skin makes vitamin D in sunlight.
86353.m: Vitamin D helps the body take in calcium.

86354.q: What happens to bones if you do not get enough calcium?
86354.e: Without enough calcium, bones become weaker. They can then break more easily.
86354.m: Too little calcium makes bones brittle.

86355.q: Which illness used to be common in Switzerland because of a lack of iodine?
86355.e: Without enough iodine, a large swelling can form on the neck. This is called a goitre.
86355.m: Iodine in salt protects against goitre.

86356.e: The thyroid gland sits at the front of the neck. It needs iodine to make important messenger substances.

86357.q: Which country was among the first to have iodised salt in 1922?
86357.e: In 1922 Switzerland was one of the first countries to introduce iodised salt. After that, illnesses caused by a lack of iodine became much rarer.
86357.m: Switzerland has had iodised salt since 1922.

86358.q: Which food naturally contains a lot of iodine?
86358.e: There is a lot of iodine in the sea. That is why sea fish and seaweed contain a lot of it.
86358.m: Sea fish contains a lot of iodine.

86359.q: Why does Swiss soil contain little iodine?
a: Glaciers and rain washed it away
86359.e: During the Ice Age and through rain, the iodine was washed out of the soil. That is why vegetables from Switzerland contain little iodine.
86359.m: Swiss soil is poor in iodine.

86360.q: What colour is the vapour of heated iodine?
86360.e: Heated iodine forms a violet vapour. The name iodine comes from the Greek word for ‘violet coloured’.

86361.q: What was tincture of iodine used for in the past?
86361.e: Tincture of iodine kills germs. In the past it was painted onto wounds.

86362.q: What colour does a potato turn when you drip iodine solution on it?
86362.e: Iodine turns starch bluish black. Potatoes contain a lot of starch.

86363.e: Pure gold shines yellow. That is why this colour is also called ‘golden’.

86364.e: Gold hardly combines with air and water. That is why it does not rust and stays shiny for a long time.

86365.q: What is a rectangular block of pure gold called?
86365.e: Gold is often cast into bars. That makes it easy to store and weigh.
86365.m: A gold bar is a block of gold.

86366.q: In which area of Switzerland do people often pan for gold in streams?
86366.e: In the streams around the Napf you can find small flakes of gold. There are also gold panning courses there.
86366.m: You can pan for gold in the Napf area.

86367.q: What is gold beaten wafer-thin called?
86367.e: Gold is so soft that it can be beaten very thin. This gold leaf is thinner than a hair.

86368.e: The Swiss National Bank owns Switzerland's gold reserves. A large part of it is kept in Switzerland.
86368.m: The National Bank looks after Switzerland's gold.

86369.e: Gold is much heavier than most substances. That is why even a small cube of gold is surprisingly heavy.
86369.m: Gold is a very heavy metal.

86370.q: What is the well-known old Swiss gold coin called?
86370.e: The gold Vreneli was minted from 1897 to 1949. It shows a woman's head.
86370.m: The Vreneli is a Swiss gold coin.

87249.q: In the shell model, what is the maximum number of electrons in the innermost shell (K shell)?
87249.e: The K shell is closest to the nucleus and is the smallest. It holds at most two electrons.
87249.m: The innermost shell holds at most two electrons.

87253.q: What is the innermost electron shell called in the shell model?
87253.e: The shells are labelled K, L, M, N and so on from the inside out. The K shell is the first.
87253.m: From the inside out, the shells are called K, L, M and N.

87254.q: Where are the electrons in the shell model?
a: In the middle of the nucleus
Between protons and neutrons in the nucleus
87254.e: In the shell model, protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus. The electrons move on shells around the nucleus.
87254.m: Electrons move on shells around the nucleus.

87255.q: How many shells are occupied in a sodium atom with 11 electrons?
87255.e: The 11 electrons are arranged like this: 2 on the first, 8 on the second and 1 on the third shell.
87255.m: A sodium atom has three occupied shells.

87256.q: How are the 13 electrons of an aluminium atom arranged on the shells (from the inside out)?
87256.e: First the first shell is filled with 2 electrons, then the second with 8. The remaining 3 electrons go on the third shell.
87256.m: Shells are filled from the inside out.

87257.q: What must an electron take in to move to a shell further out?
87257.e: Outer shells have higher energy. An electron only jumps outwards if it takes in energy, for example from heat or light.
87257.m: An electron needs energy to jump to an outer shell.

87258.q: How many valence electrons does an argon atom with 18 electrons have?
87258.e: The 18 electrons are arranged as 2, 8 and 8. So there are 8 electrons on the outermost shell.

87259.q: How many valence electrons does a carbon atom have?
87259.e: Carbon has 6 electrons: 2 on the first and 4 on the second shell. The 4 outer ones are the valence electrons.

87260.q: How many valence electrons does an oxygen atom have?
87260.e: Oxygen has 8 electrons, arranged as 2 and 6. So there are 6 electrons on the outermost shell.

87261.q: How many valence electrons does a nitrogen atom have?
87261.e: Nitrogen has 7 electrons, arranged as 2 and 5. The outer shell carries 5 electrons.

87262.q: What is the rule called by which many atoms aim to have eight electrons in their outer shell?
87262.e: ‘Octet’ comes from the Latin word for eight. With eight outer electrons, an atom is especially stable.
87262.m: The octet rule says that atoms aim for eight outer electrons.

87263.q: How are valence electrons shown in Lewis notation?
a: As dots around the element symbol
As a number under the symbol
87263.e: In Lewis notation, each valence electron is a dot next to the element symbol. A pair of electrons can also be drawn as a line.
87263.m: In Lewis notation, dots show the valence electrons.

87264.q: How many valence electrons does a chlorine atom have?
87264.e: Chlorine has 17 electrons, arranged as 2, 8 and 7. So it is only one electron short of a full outer shell.

87265.q: How many valence electrons does a phosphorus atom with 15 electrons have?
87265.e: The 15 electrons are arranged as 2, 8 and 5. So there are 5 electrons on the outermost shell.

87267.q: Which element has the atomic number 20?
87267.e: Calcium has 20 protons in its nucleus. It comes straight after potassium in the periodic table.

87268.q: Which element has the atomic number 10?
87268.e: Neon has 10 protons in its nucleus. Fluorine has 9, sodium 11 and argon 18.

87269.q: What is the atomic number of sulphur?
87269.e: Sulphur has 16 protons in its nucleus. The number 32 is the mass number of the most common sulphur isotope.

87270.q: How are the elements arranged in the periodic table?
a: By the year they were discovered
87270.e: The elements are arranged by the number of protons in the nucleus, that is, by atomic number. Hydrogen, with 1, comes first.
87270.m: The periodic table is arranged by atomic number.

87271.q: Two atoms have the same atomic number. What is true of them?
a: They belong to the same element
They have different numbers of protons
87271.e: The atomic number shows the number of protons. The same number of protons means the same element, even if the number of neutrons can differ.
87271.m: The same atomic number means the same element.

87272.q: How many electrons does an electrically neutral atom with the atomic number 12 have?
87272.e: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons. With the atomic number 12, that makes 12 electrons.
87272.m: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.

87273.q: Sodium has the atomic number 11. How many protons does a sodium atom have?
87273.e: The atomic number equals the number of protons in the nucleus. The number 23 is the mass number, which counts protons and neutrons together.
87273.m: The atomic number tells you the number of protons.

87274.q: How many main groups does the periodic table have in the classic layout?
87274.e: In the classic school numbering there are 8 main groups. Today IUPAC counts 18 groups in total, which also include the transition groups.
87274.m: In the classic layout, the periodic table has eight main groups.

87275.q: Which element is in the same main group as oxygen?
87275.e: Oxygen and sulphur are one below the other in main group 6. Both have six outer electrons.
87275.m: Oxygen and sulphur belong to main group 6.

87276.q: Which main group is also called the carbon group?
87276.e: The group is named after its first element. It also includes the metals tin and lead.
87276.m: The carbon group is main group 4.

87277.q: Which main group is aluminium in?
87277.e: Aluminium has 13 electrons, 3 of them on the outermost shell. It is the most common metal in the Earth's crust.

87278.q: How are the main groups arranged in the periodic table?
87278.e: Each main group forms a vertical column. Elements in the same column have similar chemical properties.
87278.m: Main groups run from top to bottom in the periodic table.

87279.q: What do the elements of the same main group have in common?
a: The same number of valence electrons
The same number of electron shells
87279.e: Elements in a main group have the same number of outer electrons. That is why they react in similar ways.
87279.m: Same main group means the same number of outer electrons.

87280.q: Which element is directly below carbon in the periodic table?
87280.e: Silicon comes directly after carbon in the same column. It is important for computer chips and solar cells.

87281.q: What is main group 3 also called, after its first element?
87281.e: The first element of main group 3 is boron. That is why it is called the boron group.
87281.m: Main group 3 is also called the boron group.

87282.q: From the second period on, which group of elements does each period start with on the far left?
87282.e: On the far left there is always an element with just one electron on the new outermost shell. These are the alkali metals such as lithium or sodium.
87282.m: From the second period on, every period starts with an alkali metal.

87283.q: What does the number of the period tell you?
a: The number of occupied electron shells
87283.e: All atoms in a period have the same number of electron shells. In period 2, for example, there are two shells.
87283.m: The period number shows the number of shells.

87284.q: How many elements are in the first period?
87284.e: The first period contains only hydrogen and helium. After that, the second period begins with lithium.
87284.m: The first period has only two elements.

87285.q: How many elements are in the second period?
87285.e: The second period runs from lithium to neon. That is 8 elements.
87285.m: The second period has eight elements.

87286.q: How many periods does today's periodic table have?
87286.e: The periodic table has 7 periods. Since 2016 the seventh period has been fully named, up to element 118.
87286.m: The periodic table has seven periods.

87287.e: Potassium has 19 electrons on four shells (2, 8, 8, 1). It opens period 4.
87287.m: Potassium is at the start of period 4.

87289.q: Which group of elements does each period end with on the far right?
87289.e: At the end of each period the outermost shell is full. That is true of the noble gases.
87289.m: Every period ends with a noble gas.

87290.q: Which of these metals is an alkali metal?
87290.e: Sodium is in main group 1 and so it is an alkali metal. Calcium is an alkaline earth metal.

87291.q: Why is sodium kept under paraffin oil?
a: Because it reacts violently with air and water
87291.e: Sodium reacts with the oxygen and moisture in the air. The oil protects the metal from this.
87291.m: Alkali metals are kept under oil because they react with air and water.

87292.q: Which gas forms when sodium reacts with water?
87292.e: Sodium pushes the hydrogen out of the water. This makes hydrogen gas and sodium hydroxide solution.
87292.m: Alkali metals form hydrogen gas with water.

87293.q: What is the solution like after an alkali metal has reacted with water?
87293.e: An alkaline solution forms, for example sodium hydroxide solution. Such solutions are basic, also called alkaline.
87293.m: Alkali metals form an alkaline solution with water.

87294.q: What flame colour does sodium produce?
87294.e: Sodium compounds turn a flame bright yellow. This flame colour is used to test for sodium.

87295.q: What flame colour does lithium produce?
87295.e: Lithium compounds turn a flame crimson. That is why they are also used in fireworks.

87296.q: Which metal has the lowest density of all metals?
87296.e: Lithium has a density of only about 0.53 g/cm³. It is so light that it would float on water.

87297.q: How hard is an alkali metal such as sodium?
a: You can cut it with a knife
You can only scratch it with diamond
It is as hard as steel
87297.e: Alkali metals are very soft. A freshly cut surface shines silvery but quickly tarnishes.
87297.m: Alkali metals are so soft you can cut them.

87298.q: How does the violence of the reaction with water change from lithium to caesium?
a: It increases at first, then decreases
87298.e: Going down the group, the atoms get bigger and the outer electron is given up more easily. That is why caesium reacts much more violently than lithium.
87298.m: Alkali metals react more and more violently going down the group.

87299.q: Which element is in main group 1 but is not an alkali metal?
87299.e: Like the alkali metals, hydrogen has one outer electron. But it is a non-metal and a gas.
87299.m: Hydrogen is in main group 1 but is not a metal.

87300.q: What does the word ‘halogen’ mean when translated?
87300.e: The word comes from Greek: ‘hals’ means salt and ‘gennan’ means to produce. Halogens form salts with metals.

87301.q: Which halogen is liquid at room temperature?
87301.e: Bromine is a reddish brown liquid. Apart from mercury, it is the only element that is liquid at room temperature.

87302.q: Which halogen is a solid, shiny greyish black substance at room temperature?
87302.e: Iodine forms greyish black, shiny crystals. When heated, it gives off a violet vapour.
87302.m: Iodine is solid at room temperature.

87303.q: Which main group are the halogens in?
87303.e: The halogens fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine are in main group 7, directly to the left of the noble gases.

87304.q: Which halogen is the most reactive?
87304.e: Fluorine is at the very top of the group and attracts electrons most strongly. It is the most reactive of all elements.
87304.m: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen.

87305.q: Which halogen is found as fluoride in many toothpastes?
87305.e: Fluoride hardens tooth enamel and so protects against tooth decay. That is why many toothpastes contain fluoride.
87305.m: Fluoride in toothpaste protects against tooth decay.

87306.q: Which acid forms when hydrogen chloride is dissolved in water?
87306.e: Hydrogen chloride (HCl) dissolves well in water. The solution is called hydrochloric acid; it is also found in stomach juice.
87306.m: Hydrogen chloride in water gives hydrochloric acid.

87307.q: Why is chlorine added to the water in a swimming pool?
a: To kill germs that cause disease
87307.e: Chlorine kills bacteria and other germs. That keeps the pool water hygienic.

87308.q: How many atoms make up a chlorine molecule?
87308.e: Chlorine exists as the molecule Cl₂. Two chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons.
87308.m: A chlorine molecule is made of two atoms.

87309.q: Why do noble gases hardly react with other substances?
87309.e: A full outer shell is very stable. So noble gases do not need to give up or take in electrons.
87309.m: Noble gases are unreactive because their outer shell is full.

87310.q: Which element has the lowest boiling point of all elements?
87310.e: Helium boils at about minus 269 °C, only a few degrees above absolute zero.
87310.m: Helium has the lowest boiling point of all elements.

87311.q: Which noble gas is used in very bright car headlights and flash lamps?
87311.e: In gas discharge lamps, xenon produces a very bright, almost white light. That is why they are called xenon headlights.
87311.m: Xenon gives very bright light in lamps.

87313.q: Which radioactive noble gas can get into cellars from the ground and is monitored by the Federal Office of Public Health?
87313.e: Radon forms when uranium in the ground decays. It can build up in houses especially in parts of the Alps and the Jura.
87313.m: Radon is a radioactive noble gas from the ground.

87314.q: How many valence electrons does a helium atom have?
87314.e: Helium has only 2 electrons, both on the first shell. That already makes this shell full.

87315.q: Which noble gas makes illuminated signs glow red?
87315.e: In a glass tube filled with neon, the gas glows red when electricity flows through it. That is where the word neon sign comes from.
87315.m: Neon glows red in sign tubes.

87316.q: Which noble gas is named after the Greek word for ‘hidden’?
87316.e: ‘Kryptos’ means hidden in Greek. Krypton is found in the air only in very small amounts.

87317.q: How many valence electrons do the alkaline earth metals have?
87317.e: Alkaline earth metals are in main group 2. So their outermost shell carries 2 electrons.
87317.m: Alkaline earth metals have two outer electrons.

87318.q: Which of these elements is an alkaline earth metal?
87318.e: Beryllium is the first element of main group 2. Lithium is an alkali metal, and boron and aluminium are not alkaline earth metals.
87318.m: Beryllium is the first alkaline earth metal.

87319.q: What are compounds of alkaline earth metals such as strontium and barium used for in fireworks?
a: So they can be stored longer
87319.e: Strontium compounds turn the flame red, barium compounds green. That creates the bright colours in fireworks.
87319.m: Alkaline earth metals give fireworks coloured flames.

87320.q: Which alkaline earth metal burns with a dazzling white light and was once used for flash photography?
87320.e: Magnesium burns with a very bright, white light. You must not look straight into it.
87320.m: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white light.

87321.q: Which radioactive alkaline earth metal did Marie and Pierre Curie discover in 1898?
87321.e: In 1898 the Curies discovered polonium and radium. Only radium belongs to main group 2.
87321.m: Radium is a radioactive alkaline earth metal.

87322.q: Which family of elements does calcium, found in bones and lime, belong to?
87322.e: Calcium is in main group 2 and so it is an alkaline earth metal. It is found in bones, teeth and limestone.
87322.m: Calcium is an alkaline earth metal.

87323.q: What substance is limestone, as found in the Jura, mainly made of?
87323.e: Limestone is mainly calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). It often formed from the shells of sea creatures.

87324.q: How violently does calcium react with water compared with sodium?
87324.e: Calcium reacts with water and forms hydrogen, but more calmly than sodium. Alkaline earth metals are less reactive than alkali metals.
87324.m: Alkaline earth metals react more calmly than alkali metals.

87325.q: What do all isotopes of an element have in common?
87325.e: Isotopes belong to the same element because they have the same number of protons in the nucleus. They differ only in the number of neutrons.
87325.m: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons.

87326.q: Which carbon isotope is used to find out the age of finds?
87326.e: Carbon-14 is radioactive and decays slowly, with a half-life of about 5730 years. This makes it possible to work out the age of wood or bones.
87326.m: Carbon-14 is used to date finds.

87327.q: How do isotopes of an element differ?
87327.e: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons in the nucleus. That is why they have different weights.
87327.m: Isotopes differ in the number of neutrons.

87328.q: Which element is split in nuclear power stations to produce energy?
87328.e: In nuclear power stations, uranium nuclei are split by neutrons. This releases a lot of heat, which is used to make electricity.
87328.m: Uranium nuclei are split in nuclear power stations.

87329.q: Which is the most common carbon isotope in nature?
87329.e: Around 99 per cent of natural carbon is carbon-12. It has 6 protons and 6 neutrons.

87330.q: What does the Greek word ‘isotope’ mean when translated?
87330.e: Isotopes of an element are in the same place in the periodic table because they have the same number of protons.
87330.m: Isotopes are in the same place in the periodic table.

87331.q: What are isotopes called that decay and give off radiation?
87331.e: Radioactive isotopes have an unstable nucleus. When they decay, they give off radiation.
87331.m: Radioactive isotopes decay and give off radiation.

87332.q: How do isotopes of an element differ in their chemical behaviour?
a: Hardly at all, they react almost the same
Light isotopes do not react at all
87332.e: Chemical behaviour depends on the electrons. Isotopes have the same number of electrons, so they react almost the same.
87332.m: Isotopes of an element react almost the same chemically.

87333.q: What does the mass number of an atom tell you?
87333.e: The mass number counts all the particles in the nucleus. Electrons are very light and are not counted.
87333.m: The mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons.

87334.q: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. What is its mass number?
87334.e: You add the protons and neutrons together: 11 + 12 = 23.
87334.m: For the mass number, add protons and neutrons together.

87335.q: A fluorine atom has 9 protons and the mass number 19. How many neutrons does it have?
87335.e: Neutrons = mass number minus protons, so 19 minus 9 = 10.
87335.m: The number of neutrons is the mass number minus the number of protons.

87336.q: A chlorine atom has 17 protons and the mass number 35. How many neutrons does it have?
87336.e: You work out 35 minus 17 = 18. So the atom has 18 neutrons.
87336.m: Take the protons away from the mass number and you get the neutrons.

87337.q: Where is the mass number written next to the element symbol in nuclide notation?
87337.e: The mass number goes top left, the atomic number bottom left. Top right is used, for example, for the charge of an ion.
87337.m: The mass number is written top left of the symbol.

87338.q: Uranium-238 has 92 protons. How many neutrons does it have?
87338.e: You work out 238 minus 92 = 146. So an atom of uranium-238 has 146 neutrons.
87338.m: The number after the element name is the mass number.

87339.q: Why does the periodic table give chlorine an atomic mass of about 35.5 u instead of a whole number?
a: Because it is an average of its isotopes
Because a neutron is half as heavy
87339.e: Natural chlorine is about three quarters chlorine-35 and one quarter chlorine-37. The average is around 35.5 u.
87339.m: The atomic mass in the periodic table is an average of the isotopes.

87340.q: An atom has the mass number 27 and 14 neutrons. How many protons does it have?
87340.e: Protons = mass number minus neutrons, so 27 minus 14 = 13.
87340.m: You can work out the number of protons from the mass number and the number of neutrons.

87341.q: Which country did the chemist Dmitri Mendeleev come from?
87341.e: Mendeleev came from Tobolsk in Siberia. After a period of study in Heidelberg, he worked in St Petersburg.
87341.m: Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist.

87342.q: What did Dmitri Mendeleev draw up in 1869?
a: The periodic table of the elements
87342.e: Mendeleev arranged the elements known at the time in a table. This became the periodic table.
87342.m: Mendeleev drew up the periodic table in 1869.

87343.q: Mainly by which property did Mendeleev arrange the elements?
87343.e: Protons were still unknown at the time. Mendeleev arranged the elements by their atomic weight and by similar properties.
87343.m: Mendeleev arranged the elements by atomic mass.

87344.q: What did Mendeleev do when an element did not fit into his system?
a: He left gaps for unknown elements
He put it at the end
87344.e: Mendeleev left spaces and predicted the properties of the missing elements. Later these elements really were discovered.
87344.m: Mendeleev left gaps for elements not yet discovered.

87345.q: What became clear when the elements Mendeleev had predicted were discovered?
a: They did not fit into the system at all
They did not exist at all
87345.e: Mendeleev had predicted, for example, the mass and density of the missing elements. The measurements confirmed his predictions.

87346.q: How are the elements arranged in today's periodic table?
87346.e: Today the elements are arranged by atomic number. It gives the number of protons in the nucleus.
87346.m: The periodic table is arranged by the number of protons.

87347.q: Which chemical element was named in honour of Mendeleev?
87347.e: Mendelevium was made artificially in the USA in 1955. It has the atomic number 101.
87347.m: The element mendelevium bears Mendeleev's name.

87348.q: What are the vertical columns in the periodic table called?
87348.e: Elements in the same group have similar properties. The horizontal rows are called periods.
87348.m: The columns in the periodic table are called groups.

88230.q: Between which atoms does an ionic bond typically form?
88230.e: Metal atoms give up electrons easily, and non-metal atoms take them in. The charged particles that form attract each other.
88230.m: An ionic bond usually joins a metal to a non-metal.

88231.q: Which force holds the oppositely charged ions together in an ionic bond?
88231.e: Positive and negative charges attract each other. This electrical attraction between the ions is the ionic bond.
88231.m: Opposite charges attract and hold ions together.

88232.q: What is a positively charged ion called?
88232.e: An atom that gives up electrons has more protons than electrons, so it is positively charged. In electrolysis, these ions move to the negative cathode.
88232.m: Positively charged ions are called cations.

88233.q: What is a negatively charged ion called?
88233.e: If an atom takes in extra electrons, it is negatively charged. In electrolysis, these ions move to the positive anode.
88233.m: Negatively charged ions are called anions.

88234.q: What charge does a magnesium atom get when it gives up its two outer electrons?
88234.e: Each electron given up takes a negative charge with it. After giving up two electrons, two positive charges are left over.
88234.m: Giving up electrons makes an atom positively charged.

88235.q: What is the charge of a sulphide ion, that is, a sulphur ion?
88235.e: A sulphur atom has six outer electrons and takes in two more. This gives it a double negative charge.
88235.m: Sulphur forms sulphide ions with a double negative charge.

88236.q: What is the regular arrangement of ions in a solid salt called?
88236.e: In a solid salt, the ions sit in turn in a regular pattern. This three-dimensional pattern is called an ionic lattice.
88236.m: Solid salts are made of a regular ionic lattice.

88237.q: Why do ionic compounds shatter when struck hard instead of changing shape?
a: Ions with the same charge end up side by side and repel each other
88237.e: If a blow shifts the layers of the lattice, ions with the same charge are suddenly next to each other. They repel each other and the crystal breaks.
88237.m: Ionic crystals are brittle because like charges repel.

88238.q: What is the formula of magnesium oxide, a compound of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻?
88238.e: The two positive charges of the magnesium ion exactly balance the two negative charges of the oxide ion. That is why the ions are in a ratio of 1 to 1.
88238.m: In an ionic compound the charges balance overall.

88239.q: How does a covalent bond form?
a: Two atoms share a pair of electrons
One atom gives another an electron
Metal atoms form an electron gas
88239.e: In a covalent bond, electrons belong to both atoms together. Each atom usually adds one electron to the shared pair.
88239.m: In a covalent bond, atoms share electrons.

88241.q: Between which atoms do covalent bonds typically occur?
a: Between metal and noble gas atoms
88241.e: Non-metal atoms all attract electrons fairly strongly. None of them gives up its electrons completely, so they share them.
88241.m: Non-metals usually join each other with covalent bonds.

88242.q: How many shared pairs of electrons does a double bond have?
88242.e: In a double bond, two atoms share two pairs of electrons, so four electrons in total.
88242.m: A double bond is made of two shared pairs of electrons.

88243.q: Which bond joins the two atoms in the oxygen molecule O₂?
88243.e: Each oxygen atom has six outer electrons and needs two more. That is why the two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
88243.m: In the oxygen molecule the atoms are joined by a double bond.

88244.q: What kind of particle forms when a few non-metal atoms join through covalent bonds?
88244.e: Atoms joined by covalent bonds form a closed unit such as H₂O or CO₂. These units are called molecules.
88244.m: Covalent bonds hold the atoms together in molecules.

88245.q: What is a covalent bond with three shared pairs of electrons called?
88245.e: A triple bond is very strong. It is found, for example, in the nitrogen molecule N₂.
88245.m: Three shared pairs of electrons make a triple bond.

88246.q: How many covalent bonds does a hydrogen atom form?
88246.e: Hydrogen has only one electron. With one shared pair of electrons, its shell is already full.
88246.m: A hydrogen atom always forms just one bond.

88247.q: In which substance are all the atoms joined by covalent bonds into a giant lattice?
88247.e: In diamond, every carbon atom is firmly joined to four neighbours. This continuous lattice of atoms makes it extremely hard.
88247.m: Diamond is a giant lattice of covalent bonds.

88248.q: What is the model called that describes the freely moving electrons in a metal?
88248.e: The outer electrons of the metal atoms do not belong to any one atom. They move like a gas between the positively charged metal particles.
88248.m: In a metal, the outer electrons move like an electron gas.

88249.e: Electric current is flowing charge. When a voltage is applied, the mobile electrons in the metal can easily move in one direction.
88249.m: Metals conduct electricity thanks to their mobile electrons.

88250.q: Why can metals be hammered and bent without breaking?
a: The layers of metal slide past each other without the bond breaking
Metals contain a lot of air
88250.e: The mobile electrons hold the metal particles together even after they have shifted. So the metal changes shape instead of breaking.
88250.m: Metals can be shaped because the metallic bond survives the shift.

88251.q: Which property of a metal's surface is also explained by the freely moving electrons?
88251.e: The mobile electrons at the surface reflect almost all the light that hits them. That is why freshly polished metals shine.
88251.m: Metals shine because their electrons reflect the light.

88252.q: What is a mixture of two or more metals, such as bronze, called?
88252.e: Melting metals together makes a new metal mixture with different properties. Bronze is often harder than its ingredients.
88252.m: A mixture of metals is called an alloy.

88253.q: Which metals is brass made of?
88253.e: Brass is a golden yellow alloy of copper and zinc. It is used, for example, for door handles and brass instruments.
88253.m: Brass is made from copper and zinc.

88254.q: Why are metals especially good at conducting heat?
a: The mobile electrons pass on energy quickly
88254.e: The freely moving electrons take in movement energy and carry it quickly through the whole metal. That is why a metal spoon in tea soon gets hot.
88254.m: Metals conduct heat well because their electrons carry energy.

88255.q: What are the positively charged particles called that remain in the metal lattice when the outer electrons are set free?
88255.e: When a metal atom gives its outer electrons to the shared electron gas, the rest of the atom is left with a positive charge. This remainder is called an atomic core.
88255.m: In a metal lattice, positive atomic cores sit in an electron gas.

88256.q: Which particles is a salt made of?
88256.e: In salts, positively and negatively charged particles take turns. Overall a salt is electrically neutral.
88256.m: Salts are made of cations and anions.

88257.q: What is the salt with the formula MgSO₄, also known as Epsom salt?
88257.e: Mg stands for magnesium and SO₄ for the sulphate group. The salt tastes bitter and is used, for example, in bath salts.

88258.q: Which salt is the main ingredient of gypsum?
88258.e: Gypsum is calcium sulphate with built-in water of crystallisation. It is used for walls, plaster casts and models.
88258.m: Gypsum is made of calcium sulphate.

88259.q: Why do salts usually have very high melting points?
a: The attraction between the ions is very strong
Salts contain a lot of water
Salts are made of light gases
88259.e: To melt a salt, you have to overcome the strong attraction in the ionic lattice. That needs a lot of energy and high temperatures.
88259.m: Salts only melt at high temperatures.

88260.q: What are the salts of hydrochloric acid called?
88260.e: Hydrochloric acid is a solution of hydrogen chloride (HCl). Its acid group is the chloride ion Cl⁻.
88260.m: The salts of hydrochloric acid are called chlorides.

88261.q: What are the salts of sulphuric acid called?
88261.e: The acid group of sulphuric acid is the sulphate ion. One example is copper sulphate.
88261.m: The salts of sulphuric acid are called sulphates.

88262.q: Which salt is often used as a fertiliser because it gives plants potassium?
88262.e: Plants need potassium as an important nutrient. Potassium chloride is mined for this and sold as potash fertiliser.
88262.m: Potassium chloride is an important potash fertiliser.

88263.q: What colour are copper sulphate crystals that contain water of crystallisation?
88263.e: Copper sulphate with water of crystallisation forms bright blue crystals. Without water, the salt is white.
88263.m: Copper sulphate containing water is blue.

88264.q: What is sodium chloride called in everyday life?
88264.e: Sodium chloride is the salt we use to season food. It is called table salt or cooking salt.
88264.m: Sodium chloride is our table salt.

88265.q: What happens to table salt in a hot frying pan?
88265.e: Table salt only melts at very high temperatures of about 800 degrees. So in the pan it stays solid.
88265.m: Table salt only melts at very high temperatures.

88266.q: What shape are table salt crystals under a magnifying glass?
88266.e: The ions in table salt are arranged in a regular, cube-shaped lattice. That is why the crystals look like little cubes.

88267.q: In what ratio are sodium and chloride ions found in table salt?
88267.e: A sodium ion has a single positive charge, a chloride ion a single negative charge. For the crystal to be neutral, there must be equal numbers of both.
88267.m: Table salt contains as many sodium ions as chloride ions.

88268.q: Why is it easier to float in the very salty Dead Sea than in a lake?
a: The salt water has a higher density
There are waves in the Dead Sea
88268.e: Dissolved salt makes water denser. Denser water holds the body up better, so you float almost by yourself.
88268.m: Salt water holds you up better because it is denser.

88269.q: What happens if you throw a piece of pure sodium into water?
a: It reacts violently and hydrogen forms
It simply sinks to the bottom
88269.e: Sodium is a very reactive alkali metal. With water it forms sodium hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas, often with hissing and sometimes even with fire.
88269.m: Pure sodium reacts violently with water.

88270.q: What is the most salt per day that the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends for adults?
88270.e: The WHO recommends that adults eat less than 5 grams of salt per day, about one teaspoon. Too much salt can raise blood pressure.
88270.m: Adults should eat less than 5 grams of salt per day.

88271.q: What happens to the ions when table salt dissolves in water?
a: They are surrounded by water molecules and spread out
They join up to form molecules
They break down into protons and neutrons
88271.e: The water molecules pull the ions out of the lattice and gather around them. This process is called hydration.
88271.m: When salt dissolves, the ions are surrounded by water molecules.

88272.q: What is left when salt water evaporates completely?
88272.e: When it evaporates, only the water escapes. The dissolved salt is left behind as crystals. This is how sea salt is made.
88272.m: When salt water evaporates, the salt is left behind.

88273.q: What does the electronegativity of an atom describe?
a: How strongly it attracts electrons in a bond
How many protons it has in its nucleus
88273.e: Electronegativity is a measure of how strongly an atom pulls the shared pair of electrons in a bond towards itself.
88273.m: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts bonding electrons.

88274.q: What does it mean if an atom has a high electronegativity?
a: It has a great many neutrons
88274.e: Electronegativity tells you how strongly an atom pulls the electrons in a bond towards itself. The higher the value, the stronger the pull.
88274.m: High electronegativity means a strong pull on bonding electrons.

88279.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity of all?
88279.e: Fluorine attracts electrons in a bond more strongly than any other element. It is at the top right of the periodic table.
88279.m: Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

88280.q: What is the difference in electronegativity in a bond between two identical atoms, for example in H₂?
88280.e: Two identical atoms have exactly the same electronegativity. So the difference is zero, and the pair of electrons sits exactly in the middle.
88280.m: Identical atoms pull the bonding pair equally strongly.

88281.q: What does a molecular formula tell you?
a: Which atoms and how many of each are in a molecule
How the atoms are arranged in space
How heavy a kilogram of the substance is
At what temperature the substance boils
88281.e: The molecular formula lists all the atoms in a molecule, for example H₂O. It says nothing about how the atoms are linked.
88281.m: The molecular formula counts the atoms in a molecule.

88282.q: What is the molecular formula of methane, the main part of natural gas?
88282.e: A methane molecule is made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. It is the simplest hydrocarbon.

88283.q: How many atoms are in one molecule of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆)?
88283.e: You count 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms. 6 + 12 + 6 makes 24 atoms.
88283.m: Adding up the numbers in the molecular formula gives the number of atoms.

88284.q: What is the molecular formula of ammonia?
88284.e: An ammonia molecule is made of one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms. It has a sharp smell and is used for fertiliser.

88285.q: Which substance has the molecular formula C₂H₆O?
88285.e: Ethanol, the alcohol in drinks, is made of 2 carbon, 6 hydrogen and one oxygen atom. It is found in wine and beer.
88285.m: The alcohol in drinks has the molecular formula C₂H₆O.

88286.q: How many atoms in total are in one molecule of sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)?
88286.e: H₂SO₄ contains 2 hydrogen atoms, 1 sulphur atom and 4 oxygen atoms. 2 + 1 + 4 makes 7.
88286.m: No number after a symbol means one atom.

88287.q: What is the formula of carbon dioxide?
88287.e: Carbon dioxide has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. The prefix ‘di’ means two.
88287.m: Carbon dioxide has the formula CO₂.

88288.q: What does the small 2 in the formula H₂O mean?
a: A molecule contains two hydrogen atoms
The molecule has a double charge
88288.e: The small number applies to the symbol directly in front of it. So a water molecule has two H atoms and one O atom.
88288.m: Small numbers count the atoms of the symbol in front.

88290.q: What does a structural formula show in addition to the molecular formula?
a: How the atoms are joined to each other
How many neutrons the atoms have
88290.e: In the structural formula you can see which atom is bonded to which. This lets you tell apart substances with the same molecular formula.
88290.m: The structural formula shows how the atoms are linked.

88291.q: What does a line between two atoms in a structural formula mean?
88291.e: In the structural formula, each line stands for a shared pair of electrons, that is, a bond. This shows which atoms are joined.
88291.m: A line in a structural formula is a bond.

88292.q: How many bond lines does the structural formula of ethane (C₂H₆) show?
88292.e: Each of the six hydrogen atoms is attached to a carbon atom by a line. There is also a line between the two carbon atoms: 6 + 1 makes 7.
88292.m: In a structural formula, each line stands for a single bond.

88293.q: What is the structural formula of carbon dioxide?
88293.e: The carbon atom sits in the middle and has a double bond to each oxygen atom. The molecule is straight.
88293.m: In carbon dioxide, the carbon is in the middle.

88294.q: What shape is a water molecule?
88294.e: The two lone pairs of electrons on the oxygen push the two hydrogen atoms together. That is why the molecule is bent like a V.

88295.q: How many bond lines come from each carbon atom in a structural formula?
88295.e: Carbon has four outer electrons, so it forms four bonds. A double bond counts as two lines.
88295.m: Carbon always has four bonds in structural formulas.

88296.q: Which molecular formula belongs to the structural formula H-O-O-H?
88296.e: You count two hydrogen and two oxygen atoms. The substance is called hydrogen peroxide and is used for bleaching.
88296.m: You can count the molecular formula from the structural formula.

88298.q: Where do hydrogen bonds act in liquid water?
a: Between the water and the air
88298.e: A hydrogen atom of one molecule is attracted by the oxygen atom of a neighbouring molecule. That way the molecules loosely cling together.
88298.m: Hydrogen bonds link water molecules to each other.

88299.q: What is the weak attraction called that makes water molecules stick to each other?
88299.e: The hydrogen atom of one water molecule is attracted by the oxygen atom of a neighbouring molecule. This attraction is called a hydrogen bond.
88299.m: Water molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds.

88300.q: Why does ice float on liquid water?
a: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules further apart
Ice contains trapped bubbles of nitrogen
Ice is repelled magnetically by water
88300.e: When water freezes, the hydrogen bonds arrange the molecules into an open lattice with gaps. That is why ice has a lower density than water.
88300.m: Ice is lighter than water because its lattice has gaps.

88301.q: At what temperature does water have its greatest density?
88301.e: Water is densest at around 4 °C. That is why in winter water at 4 degrees gathers at the bottom of lakes, and fish survive there.

88302.q: What holds the two strands of DNA together?
88302.e: The bases of the two strands face each other in pairs and are joined by two or three hydrogen bonds. This allows the DNA to be separated for copying.
88302.m: Hydrogen bonds hold the DNA double helix together.

88303.q: How strong is a hydrogen bond compared with a covalent bond?
88303.e: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules and is only a small fraction as strong as a covalent bond. That is why it is easy to break.
88303.m: Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds.

88304.q: Why can pond skaters walk on the surface of water?
a: Hydrogen bonds create a high surface tension
The water is frozen at the surface
The insects are lighter than air
There is low pressure under the surface
88304.e: At the surface, the water molecules pull strongly together through hydrogen bonds. This forms a kind of thin skin that can carry small animals.
88304.m: Hydrogen bonds give water a high surface tension.

88305.q: What happens to the hydrogen bonds when water boils?
88305.e: When water boils, the molecules get so much energy that the hydrogen bonds break. The molecules separate and fly off as steam.
88305.m: When water boils, the hydrogen bonds between the molecules break.

a: A molecule with a positive end and a negative end
A molecule made of exactly two atoms
A molecule that is always a gas
88306.e: If one atom attracts the bonding electrons more strongly, a negative part forms there. If the centres of charge are apart, the molecule has two poles.
88306.m: A dipole has a positive end and a negative end.

88307.q: Which well-known molecule is a dipole?
88307.e: In the water molecule, oxygen attracts the electrons more strongly than hydrogen. Molecules made of two identical atoms have no poles.

88308.q: Which simple experiment shows that water is made of dipole molecules?
a: A thin stream of water is bent by a rubbed plastic rod
Water gets cold in the fridge
An ice cube melts in your hand
88308.e: The rubbed rod is electrically charged. The water molecules turn the matching end towards it, and the stream bends.
88308.m: A charged rod bends a stream of water.

88309.q: Which end of a water molecule is partly negatively charged?
